## The question this category answers

> How do you issue a unit that holds a peg when its backing is volatile, held by someone else, and can become worth less than the unit?

## The category residue the original lane recorded

Two structural failures. (1) Monetary policy. Every protocol here sets a rate to defend a peg — Sky's Stability Fee and SSR, USDD's Stability Fees, Lista's, crvUSD's automatic controller, Liquity V2's borrower-chosen rates. The vocabulary's Stability register contains Rd, Ps and As: a redemption right, a 1:1 swap, and quantity adjustment. There is no price-of-credit instrument in it at all, and that is the instrument all five actually use. (2) The synthetic-dollar family is outside the register entirely. Ethena ($3,873M) + Falcon Finance ($1,253M) + Solstice ($507M) = $5,633M, which is larger than Sky, and none of them are CDPs: the backing is a hedged position on venues the protocol does not control. Expressing that family needs at minimum three new elements — off-exchange custody/mirroring, off-protocol revenue capture, and a maintained-neutrality invariant — none of which exist even as candidates. Separately: Sky, USDD and Lista CDP form a strict nesting (Lista subset-of USDD subset-of Sky, differing only by At, Xf and Fd), so three protocols and $7.3B collapse into one Maker skeleton the vocabulary cannot tell apart. The Dutch auction used by all three is reachable only through contested Da, which given 3-of-5 usage is the strongest promotion candidate in the contested register. And Frax, named in the brief as an exemplar, is now $42.6M and filed by DefiLlama under 'Algo-Stables' — the algorithmic design As was presumably written for has left the top of the market entirely.

## Lane narrative

**What the section introduction should say.** Every member issues a unit meant to hold a peg against backing that is volatile, held by someone else, and can become worth less than the unit. The corpus records a *single* residue for the category — no price-of-credit instrument — and that turns out to be wrong in shape rather than wrong in fact.

**The finding: the rate gap is four gaps.** There are four distinct rate instruments among the five protocols, and the corpus files one under the wrong heading:

1. a **deployed bounded-delegate rate setter** — an agent sets the borrow rate, the savings rate and the savings-reserve rate within min, max and step bounds, with no executive vote;
2. an administered rate keyed to **external benchmarks**, including a central-bank policy rate;
3. a **closed-loop controller on peg error**;
4. **borrower-chosen** rates, priced per position by the borrower — which is not an instrument the protocol holds at all.

**Why (1) matters beyond this category.** It is the yield lane's delegated allocation mandate in different dress — named agent, bounded quantity, cap, step limit, revocation — bounding a *rate* rather than an allocation. Two lanes, different categories, different evidence, same five-part schema. That is the run's first cross-lane convergence and the strongest argument for a level above the element.

**Also.** The control-plane register is a bigger gap here than the rate one. One protocol's core is BUSL-1.1 until 2027-09-01. Two recorded residues for one protocol are refuted outright — its liquidation is standard, not gas-only. One protocol has no public repository for its CDP core at all, so its entire control plane is UNKNOWN.
